title: The Atmosphere
keyIdea: The Earth is wrapped in a layer of air called the atmosphere. Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. Air is matter, so it has weight, and the air above us presses down on everything: this is air pressure. Pressure is highest at sea level and falls as you climb, because there is less air above you. The atmosphere has layers. Almost all weather happens in the lowest one, the troposphere. Above it, the ozone layer in the stratosphere soaks up most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light, and the air as a whole keeps Earth warm enough for life, about 15 °C on average instead of about −18 °C.
familyTip: Next time you fly or drive up a big hill, take a sealed packet of crisps or a closed plastic bottle with you. Look at it at the top and again at the bottom, and talk about why the air outside makes it puff up or squash in.

visual.caption: Which layer of the atmosphere? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fill 100 squares of air, weigh a pumped balloon, carry a sealed packet up a mountain, sort the layers, test the ozone shield and heat blanket.

kid: The Earth is wrapped in a thin layer of air. It is called the atmosphere. Air is a mix of gases. In every 100 parts, about 78 are nitrogen and 21 are oxygen. The last 1 part is argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.
Air is matter, so it has weight. Pump air into a balloon and that side of a balance goes down. All the air above us presses on us and on everything else. This push is called air pressure.
Air pressure is highest at sea level. Climb a mountain and there is less air above you, so it pushes less. A sealed bag of crisps puffs up at the top, then gets squashed again at the bottom.

The atmosphere has layers. Almost all weather is in the lowest layer, the troposphere. Higher up, the ozone layer soaks up most of the Sun's harmful UV light. The air also keeps heat in, like a blanket, so Earth is warm enough for life.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. In England, Year 5 Earth and space and Year 4 states of matter (air as a gas that has mass) underpin this topic, and Key Stage 3 geography and science return to the atmosphere's composition and layers. NGSS 5-ESS2-1 asks pupils to model how the atmosphere interacts with land, water and living things. Pupils should know the atmosphere is the layer of air around Earth, that air has weight and exerts pressure, that weather happens in the troposphere, and that the atmosphere shields and warms the planet.

Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide. Sea-level pressure averages about 1013 hPa and roughly halves for every 5.5 km of height; at the top of Everest it is about a third. The troposphere reaches about 12 km on average (less at the poles, more at the equator) and holds most of the air's mass and nearly all its water vapour. The stratosphere (to about 50 km) holds the ozone layer, about 15 to 35 km up. Meteors mostly burn up in the mesosphere (50 to 85 km); the aurora and the space station are in the thermosphere. Without the greenhouse effect Earth's average would be about −18 °C rather than about 15 °C.

Common mistakes. Many children think air is mostly oxygen. Some think air weighs nothing, or that air makes things lighter; a helium balloon floats only because helium is lighter than air. Some think pressure is higher up a mountain because it is nearer the sky. Others put clouds and weather in a high layer, or think Earth would be hotter with no air because nothing would block the Sun. In the lab each slip meets a square count, a balance, a packet, a layer card or a thermometer that shows it.

practice.prompt: Which gas makes up most of the air?
choices: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
practice.hint: Think of the 100 squares. Which gas filled about 78 of them?
practice.explain: About 78% of the air is nitrogen. Oxygen is about 21%, and carbon dioxide is far less than 1%.

practice.prompt: In {=n*100} litres of air, about how many litres are nitrogen?
practice.hint: About 78 in every 100 litres of air is nitrogen. How many hundreds are there?
practice.explain: {=n*100} litres is {n} lots of 100, and each 100 has about 78 litres of nitrogen: {n} × 78 = {=n*78} litres.

practice.prompt: In {=n*100} litres of air, about how many litres are oxygen?
practice.hint: About 21 in every 100 litres of air is oxygen.
practice.explain: Each 100 litres has about 21 litres of oxygen, so {n} lots of 100 have {n} × 21 = {=n*21} litres.

practice.prompt: A sealed bag of crisps puffs up at the top of a mountain. Why?
choices: There is less air above, so less air pressure pushes on the bag
The air at the top is heavier
The crisps make gas as they get colder
practice.hint: Is there more or less air above you when you climb higher?
practice.explain: Higher up, less air is above you, so the air pressure outside the bag is lower. The air inside pushes out and the bag puffs up.

practice.prompt: In which layer of the atmosphere do clouds and rain form?
choices: The troposphere, the lowest layer
The stratosphere, with the ozone layer
The thermosphere, where the space station flies
practice.hint: Weather happens close to the ground. Which layer starts at the ground?
practice.explain: Almost all weather, including clouds and rain, happens in the troposphere, the layer from the ground to about 12 km up.

pool.prompt: You pump air into one of two balloons on a balance. What happens?
choices: The side with the full balloon goes down
The side with the full balloon goes up
It stays level, because air weighs nothing
pool.hint: Air is matter. Does matter have weight?
pool.explain: Air has mass, so it has weight. The balloon with extra air in it is heavier, so its side goes down.

choices: At sea level
At the top of a high mountain
It is the same everywhere
pool.hint: Air pressure comes from the weight of the air above you.
pool.explain: At sea level the most air is above you, pressing down, so the pressure is highest there. It falls as you climb.

pool.prompt: What does the ozone layer do?
choices: Soaks up most of the Sun's harmful UV light
Makes clouds and rain
Holds the air close to Earth
pool.hint: Think of the purple shield in the lab. What did it stop?
pool.explain: The ozone layer, in the stratosphere, absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet light. Gravity, not ozone, holds the air to Earth.

pool.prompt: Mia says Earth would be hotter with no air, because nothing would block the Sun. What is wrong?
choices: Heat would escape to space, so Earth would be much colder
Nothing, it would be hotter
The Sun would stop shining on Earth
pool.hint: The air acts like a blanket. What does a blanket do at night?
pool.explain: Sunlight would still get in, but without the air's blanket the heat would escape. Earth would average about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C.

pool.prompt: In {=n*100} litres of air, about how many litres are NOT nitrogen?
pool.hint: About 78 in every 100 litres is nitrogen. What is left from each 100?
pool.explain: Each 100 litres has about 100 − 78 = 22 litres of other gases, mostly oxygen. So {n} × 22 = {=n*22} litres.

pool.prompt: One cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kg. About what mass of air is in a room that holds {=n*10} cubic metres of air, in kg?
pool.hint: Ten cubic metres of air have a mass of about 10 × 1.2 = 12 kg. How many lots of 10 are there?
pool.explain: {=n*10} cubic metres is {n} lots of 10, and each 10 has a mass of about 12 kg, so the air has a mass of about {n} × 12 = {=n*12} kg.

pool.prompt: Where do most meteors burn up?
choices: In the mesosphere, 50 to 85 km up
In the troposphere, near the ground
On the ground, when they land
pool.hint: It is the layer above the ozone layer, where there is just enough air to heat them.
pool.explain: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere, about 50 to 85 km up, as they rub through the thin air there.

choices: The layer of air that surrounds the Earth
Only the clouds in the sky
The empty space between the planets
pool.hint: It is a layer that wraps the whole planet. What is it made of?
pool.explain: The atmosphere is the layer of air, a mix of gases, held around the Earth by gravity. Clouds are just one part of it.

pool.prompt: Why is it harder to breathe at the top of a very high mountain?
choices: The air is thinner, so each breath has less oxygen in it
There is no oxygen at all up there
The air there is mostly carbon dioxide
pool.hint: The mix of gases is the same, but how much air is in each breath?
pool.explain: The air is still about 21% oxygen, but it is thinner: at the top of Everest each breath holds only about a third as much air as at sea level.
